cli.identity.keep: Same installation (move/restore): identity kept, binding updated
cli.identity.new: New installation: new installationId, projects preserved
cli.init.previewOnly: Preview only: package/image trust and availability remain unverified; nothing was installed.
cli.init.evidenceOnly: Read-only observations: package bytes and local image availability measured; no operator approval, publisher verification or installation.
cli.init.applied: Installation result (explicit local trust; publisher verification remains unavailable):
cli.init.policyUpgrade.preview: The first-run policy (revision {revision}) can take the current first-run rules below; nothing was written. Apply: deckent init policy --scope {scope} --upgrade --apply --expect {revision}{person}
cli.init.policyUpgrade.upgraded: The first-run policy now has the current first-run rules below (the previous documents are archived); everything else was kept.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.current: This first-run policy already has the current first-run rules; nothing to do.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.unavailable: This policy is not a first-run policy naming you, so it is not changed; add the current first-run rules with your own policy authority (deckent policy upgrade --template current --preview shows them).
cli.init.policyUpgrade.notOwner: Only the installation's owner (the user who owns its policy files) may upgrade it here; nothing was written. Use the governed path: deckent policy upgrade --template current --scope {scope} --preview
cli.init.policyUpgrade.conflict: The policy changed since the preview (now revision {revision}); nothing was written. Preview again.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.conflicts: Kept as they are (same id, other content; review them): {ids}
cli.init.policyUpgrade.wireRules: Kept, but no longer used for MCP calls (an MCP call is now allowed per server, mcp-server): {ids}
cli.init.policyUpgrade.previewPerson: This hand-built policy (revision {revision}) can give the named person the current first-run rules below; nothing was written. Apply: deckent init policy --scope {scope} --upgrade --apply --expect {revision}{person}
cli.init.policyUpgrade.upgradedPerson: The policy now gives the named person the current first-run rules below (the previous documents are archived); every existing rule was kept.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.currentPerson: The named person already has the current first-run rules in this policy; nothing to do.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.handBuilt: This policy was not written by the first-run template, so it was not changed. As its owner, name the person to upgrade: deckent init policy --scope {scope} --upgrade --preview --person <issuer>/<subject>. People it names in {scope}: {people}
cli.init.policyUpgrade.serviceIdentityCh: The runtime service identity (service.identity) or the configuration changed since this plan was made; nothing was written to the policy. Preview again: deckent init policy --scope {scope} --upgrade --preview
cli.init.policyUpgrade.serviceIdentityUn: This apply needs the --expect value the preview printed (it binds the policy revision and the runtime service identity); nothing was written. Preview again: deckent init policy --scope {scope} --upgrade --preview
cli.init.policyUpgrade.serviceIdentityWr: Runtime service identity set: service.identity = {scope}/{service}. A service that is already running reads it only at its next start: stop it once (Ctrl+C on deckent runtime serve; a service the terminal started also stops by itself after its idle time, 15 minutes by default), then deckent runtime restart and deckent runtime shutdown work.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.serviceIdentityPl: Apply also sets the missing runtime service identity: service.identity = {scope}/{service}.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.serviceIdentityOt: service.identity names scope {scope} (service {service}), not this scope; it was kept as it is. deckent runtime restart stops that service only with a shutdown grant in {scope}.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.serviceIdentityNo: The runtime service identity could not be set ({code}); the policy result above stands. Check deckent config explain service.identity, then run this upgrade again.
cli.init.policyUpgrade.personNotNamed: {person} is not named on any allow rule of scope {scope}, so nothing was written. People it names there: {people}
cli.init.pool.preview: Pool {pool}: execution slots {execution}, in-flight slots {inFlight}; nothing was written. Apply: deckent init pool --scope {scope} --apply. Then re-run /do.
cli.init.pool.created: Created pool {pool}: execution slots {execution}, in-flight slots {inFlight}. Re-run /do.
cli.init.pool.current: Pool {pool} is already configured: execution slots {execution}, in-flight slots {inFlight}. Re-run /do.
cli.init.pool.conflict: Pool {pool} was not changed: stored slots {storedExecution}/{storedInFlight}, configured slots {execution}/{inFlight}. Review the configuration; use deckent pool set-capacity for capacity changes before re-running /do.
cli.init.pool.notOwner: Pool {pool} was not changed. Only the owner of both policy and bindings files may provision it. Ask the installation owner to run deckent init pool --scope {scope} --preview.
cli.init.pool.ledgerVersion: Pool {pool} was not changed: ledger version {version} is not the current version. Use the installation upgrade path, then run deckent init pool --scope {scope} --preview.
cli.init.pool.unavailable: Pool {pool} is unavailable ({reason}); nothing was written. Check admission configuration and the existing installation ledger, then run deckent init pool --scope {scope} --preview.
cli.init.registry.preview: First registry preview; no registry or configuration was written. Re-run the same command with --apply after review.
cli.init.registry.applied: First admission registry created. Next: deckent init pool --scope <id> --preview, then --apply.
